title: Between, Under, Not: inter-, sub-, non-
objectives: I can use the prefixes inter-, sub-, and non- to work out the meaning of new words.
I can split ten words into a prefix and a base and tell what each part means.
I can use these words in a story about a trip and in a report.
I can write sentences that show the exact meaning of each prefix.
rationale: Inter-, sub-, and non- appear throughout informational texts and school subjects, and each example has a visible base that students can separate and name (state, national, section, view, marine, divide, heading, fiction, sense, stop). Students first see the prefix, then the base, and then check the meaning against a sentence. Reject from unit 3 is revisited as another word whose prefix students can separate, and the story words dejected and conflict return in review. The passage is a short narrative of a museum trip where all ten words are used naturally.

words.def: Joining places in different parts of a country.
words.ex: The family drove along the interstate highway all the way from Ohio to Kentucky.
words.ex2: An interstate bus can carry you across several state lines in a day.
words.nonExample: A road that stays inside one small town is not interstate.

apps.academic: An interstate highway links cities in different states.
apps.spoken: We took the interstate to get to Grandma's house.
apps.writing: Use interstate for roads or trips that cross from one state to another.

cloze.s: The truck driver took the ___ highway that crossed from Texas into Oklahoma.

cloze2.s: An ___ bus rolled across three state lines before sunset.

misuse.s: The interstate road stayed on one tiny street inside the town and never reached another state.
misuse.why: Interstate means between states; a road that never leaves one town is not interstate.

words.ex2: Ships from around the world fill the international harbor.

apps.academic: International trade moves goods from one country to another.

cloze.s: Athletes from forty countries gathered for the ___ games.

cloze2.s: The ___ airport has flights to cities on every continent.

words.def: A place where two or more roads cross.
words.ex: The crossing guard stood at the intersection to help students cross.
words.ex2: Draw a line and then a second line, and mark the intersection where they meet.
words.nonExample: A long straight road with no cross street has no intersection.

apps.spoken: Meet me at the intersection near the park.
apps.writing: Use intersection for the place where roads or lines cross.

words.ex2: Before the interview, Lia wrote five questions for the librarian.
words.nonExample: A speech given by one person without questions is not an interview.

misuse.why: An interview has questions and answers between two people; a one-person talk does not.

words.def: A ship that can travel underwater.
words.ex: The submarine slowly dived beneath the waves.
words.ex2: Scientists used a small submarine to explore the deep ocean floor.
words.nonExample: A sailboat that stays on the surface is not a submarine.

apps.academic: A submarine can stay underwater for a long time because it carries its own air supply.
apps.spoken: We toured a submarine at the museum.
apps.writing: Use submarine for a ship that moves under the water.

cloze.s: The ___ sank below the waves and stayed hidden under the water for days.

cloze2.s: A small ___ carried scientists to the bottom of the sea to study fish.

misuse.s: The submarine soared above the clouds and landed on a mountain.
misuse.why: A submarine travels under the water; it does not fly or land on a mountain.

words.def: To split a part into smaller parts again.
words.ex: The farmer will subdivide the field into four small gardens.
words.ex2: Mr. Ruiz had to subdivide the class into small teams for the project.
words.nonExample: Putting two pieces together is not subdividing.

apps.academic: In math, you can subdivide a unit into smaller equal parts.
apps.spoken: Let's subdivide the job so everyone has a part.
apps.writing: Use subdivide when a piece is cut into smaller pieces.

cloze.s: To make room for more houses, the builder decided to ___ the large lot into six small ones.

cloze2.s: The teacher will ___ each group into pairs for the next activity.

misuse.s: To subdivide the pizza, he glued all eight slices back into one large circle.
misuse.why: To subdivide is to split into smaller parts; gluing slices together does the opposite.

words.def: A smaller title under a main title.
words.ex2: A good subheading helps readers find facts quickly in a long article.
words.nonExample: The main title at the top of a page is not a subheading.

apps.academic: A nonfiction text uses subheadings to tell what each part is about.
apps.spoken: I used the subheadings to find the answer fast.

words.def: Writing about real people, places, and facts.

words.ex2: She preferred nonfiction because she liked learning real facts about space.

cloze2.s: A biography is ___ because it tells the true story of a real person's life.

words.def: Words or ideas that have no meaning or are silly.

words.ex2: The poem was pure nonsense, full of words that nobody had ever heard.

apps.writing: Use nonsense for words or ideas that do not make sense.

cloze.s: The toddler's happy babbling was ___, but everyone laughed anyway.

cloze2.s: A rhyme full of invented words may seem like ___ at first, but it can still be fun.

passage.title: A Day at the Submarine Museum
paras: Our class rode a bus on the interstate highway to a harbor museum. The drive was nonstop for an hour, and by the time we arrived, we were ready to move. At the busy intersection near the museum, the driver waited for the light to turn green.
Inside, a guide welcomed us. "A submarine is a ship that can travel under the water," she said. Because the group was large, she decided to subdivide us into three smaller teams.

In the museum shop, I found a nonfiction book about sea life. Its chapters had subheadings that made the facts easy to find. A picture book about talking fish was pure nonsense, but I loved it anyway.

Outside, we met a sailor from another country. The harbor welcomes international ships from many nations. Our teacher let us interview the sailor, and each team asked one question. I wrote down his answers for our class report.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "intersection" most nearly means
qs.why: The bus driver waits at the place where roads meet and the light turns green.

qs.q: Why did the guide subdivide the group?
choices: She wanted to start a race.
The group was large, so smaller teams worked better.
qs.why: The text says the group was large, so she split it into three smaller teams.

qs.q: Why did the writer say the talking-fish book was nonsense?
choices: It was too hard to read.
It was about a real sailor.
The fish could not really talk.
qs.why: Talking fish cannot be real, so the story is silly and made up.

qs.q: Which detail shows that the sailor came from another country?
choices: The sailor wrote a class report.
The harbor welcomes international ships from many nations.
qs.why: The harbor welcomes ships from many nations, and the sailor is described as from another country.

qs.q: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: A class trip to a museum where students learn and use new words
qs.why: The narrator describes events on a museum trip and uses the words in context.

teacher.overview: Students learn the prefixes inter-, sub-, and non- through ten words, read a museum-trip story, and practice splitting words into prefix and base and writing sentences with each word.

notes.va.interstate.adj: State is the base. Students sometimes only know the word as a road; show it also means between states, as in an interstate trip.
notes.va.international.adj: International = inter- + national. Ask what national means, then what international adds.
notes.va.intersection.n: Section means a part cut off. Draw two crossing lines and mark the intersection. Link to geometry.
notes.va.interview.n: Interview = inter- + view: a view between two people. Role-play an interview with a partner and a list of questions.
notes.va.submarine.n: Marine means of the sea. Contrast sub- (under) with super- (above) if students ask; sub- also appears in subway.
notes.va.subdivide.v: Sub- here means a smaller part. Use a paper rectangle: divide, then subdivide the parts.
notes.va.subheading.n: Use a real article to find the heading and the subheadings. Ask what each subheading promises.
notes.va.nonfiction.n: Non- means not. Sort book titles into fiction and nonfiction. Note that non- does not mean the opposite of everything: nonfiction can be exciting.
notes.va.nonsense.n: Nonsense is not only silly; it is also meaningless. Students may enjoy writing a short nonsense poem and then a sensible one.
notes.va.nonstop.adj: Non- + stop: not stopping. Use a flight map to show a nonstop route versus one with a stop.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The word is subdivide. I see the prefix sub- and the base divide. Sub- can mean under or a smaller part, and divide means split. So subdivide means to split into smaller parts. In the passage, the guide subdivides the large group into three teams, and that fits.'
discuss: Which prefix is easiest to spot? Which is hardest?
Can you think of other words with inter-, sub-, or non-?
misconceptions: Non- always means the opposite instead of not.
Intersection and interstate are the same word.
Nonsense is a made-up word with no use.
extend: Make a word wheel with inter-, sub-, and non- and find five more words in a dictionary.
Write a two-paragraph museum report with at least three subheadings.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the prefix meanings two days later, again at one week, and reuse reject, dejected, and conflict from earlier units when students split prefix and base in new words.

wida.oral: Partner A says a word from this unit. Partner B says the prefix, the base, and the meaning. Switch roles.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (sin escalas for nonstop, tontería, subtítulo, interestatal) not reviewed by a native speaker; interestatal is rare outside the United States context.
Base meanings (section = a part cut off, view = see, marine = of the sea) are standard but should be confirmed against a classroom dictionary.
The passage is invented fiction; the museum is not a real place.
